title: What I learned listening to a principal coach
author: Rod J. Naquin
summary: Rod Naquin shares the findings of his dissertation, Leadership Talk, which asks what separates energizing coaching conversations from ones that leave teachers feeling processed. He shadowed one Louisiana elementary principal for a full day, recorded two one-on-one coaching sessions and two student-placement committee meetings, and interviewed her and two teachers. The principal behaved very differently depending on the room: up to 75 percent of her questions were open-ended in one-on-ones, while in one committee meeting 91 percent were closed and directive language outnumbered collaborative language 12 to 1. A second meeting on the same protocol was far more collaborative, so he concludes that the moment, not the structure, decided the conversation. Under time pressure reflection disappeared first, and teachers credited her with real growth that she was more modest about. His advice is to protect time for reflection and to ask teachers how coaching felt.
points: The same principal coached very differently one-on-one than in a committee meeting, with up to 75 percent open-ended questions in one-on-ones and 91 percent closed questions in one committee meeting.
The protocol did not determine the tone, since an identical meeting structure produced much more collaboration on another occasion.
Time pressure removes reflection first, which means the parts of coaching most tied to teacher growth are the first to be lost.
Teachers and the principal agreed that trust, being asked before being told, and a hierarchy that is present but not heavy matter most.
Leaders should protect reflection time and ask teachers how coaching felt, rather than relying only on self-report.
quotes: Most of us have sat through a coaching conversation with an administrator. Some leave you energized; others leave you feeling processed.

In the one-on-one sessions, up to 75 percent of her questions were open-ended, and she sat beside teachers rather than across a desk. In one committee meeting, 91 percent of her questions were closed, and directive language outnumbered collaborative language 12 to 1.

The structure didn’t decide the conversation; the moment did. And under time pressure, reflection didn’t just shrink. It disappeared, which means the parts of coaching most tied to teacher growth were the first to go.
Teachers and the principal agreed on what mattered: trust, being asked before being told, and a hierarchy that’s present but not heavy.
Teachers also described her cultural responsiveness in detail, unprompted, even though my interview protocol never asked her about it.
For principals and district leaders, the lesson is to protect time for reflection, because a packed schedule quietly strips it out.
Better coaching isn’t just about learning more techniques. It’s about helping leaders see, name, and trust the responsive practice many of them are already doing.
